## Completion state

This epic is complete. It replaces the fragmented Jira-specific operator surface with one provider-neutral, Python-first bridge surface while retaining every live legacy contract needed by existing workflows and environments. Twenty descendants are closed; their code is merged, including final Gerrit change 1595, and the completed tree is present at ref `694cf894def36241724e7049e3308d782037ef6d`.

## Product and compatibility decisions

- The canonical noun is `bridge`; the design is intentionally tracker-neutral.
- `bridge preview` and `bridge sync` are primary. `reconcile` remains an explicit compatibility adapter with its historical safe dry-run default.
- Canonical verbs are setup, check-access, fsck, status, preview, sync, pause, and resume.
- `bridge-status` remains a compatibility entrypoint. The audited-dead `purge-bridge` spelling remains removed.
- Canonical exits are 0, 1, and 2. Legacy adapters retain historical 3, 4, and 75 translations where older workflows and environments depend on them.
- Canonical operational selection uses `--max-changes`, `--only`, `--except`, and `--max-age`, with user-facing help that does not expose engine internals.
- Pause state is remote-persisted, includes a reason, and remains readable by mixed-version fleets.
- Destructive repair and normal bridge operation no longer require the GitHub-specific `gh` CLI.

The default inversion is deliberate and covered through real entrypoints: argument-less `reconcile` remains non-mutating, while argument-less `bridge sync` is the canonical mutating command. Compatibility is implemented as explicit adapters rather than a naive alias.

## Three interfaces

All supported interfaces expose the bridge functionality through shared Python services:

- Python library: public imports provide the bridge operations and preserve legacy reconcile behavior.
- CLI: `rebar bridge ...` is canonical; retained commands and flags normalize through compatibility adapters.
- MCP server: MCP tools expose the same bridge capabilities and route through the same library/core contracts.

Automated workflows use the same Python core. Reads, preview, and status remain compatible while outbound sync/delivery selects its intended strictness explicitly. No surface has a private reimplementation of bridge semantics.

## Three install paths

The feature works from all supported installation routes:

- brew installs the packaged `rebar` CLI and Python implementation.
- pip installs the same library and console entrypoints.
- MCP-server installation runs the same bridge library/core through `rebar-mcp`.

No supported path depends on an editable checkout, repository-only helper, ambient Python, or a newly introduced shell script. Runtime ownership is Python; YAML, Jenkins, and GitLab files remain thin declarative wrappers.

## Portable automation and delivery

The bridge is runner-neutral across local execution, GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI, and bare environments. Provider wrappers share code-derived exit behavior, secrets vocabulary, and timeout policy. Full-depth execution succeeds; shallow history fails with a named diagnostic. Jenkins secret use avoids Groovy interpolation. GitLab configuration is validated offline against its vendored pinned schema. Required shellcheck coverage validates the unavoidable provider shell bodies as test artifacts; shellcheck is not a runtime dependency and bridge behavior is not implemented in shell.

Tickets-branch delivery is also Python-owned:

- `src/rebar/_store/push.py` owns CAS retry, fetch-and-merge recovery, strict failure classification, and the terminal push budget.
- The locked Python `commit-and-push` entrypoint owns staging, commit identity/subject, and delivery.
- The bridge workflow invokes `rebar bridge run`; the canary invokes the Python push adapter once.
- Workflow-local CAS loops and the stale raw-git exemption rationale are absent.
- Existing Python, CLI, MCP, importer, and ticket-store callers remain best effort unless explicitly adapted.

## ADR numbering and indexing

ADR 0092 records the bridge-primary vocabulary and explicit compatibility-adapter decision. It complies with the current ADR convention:

- the filename is `docs/adr/0092-bridge-primary-vocabulary-compatibility-adapters.md`;
- the heading uses the same unique four-digit number;
- `docs/adr/README.md` contains the matching 0092 index entry;
- the repository ADR collision/index gate recognizes the file;
- later changes updated ADR 0092 and the older ADR 0027/0070 references without creating a duplicate or out-of-index decision.

## Verification evidence

The merged descendant changes passed Gerrit LLM review and CI. The combined RED-first and held-out coverage includes:

- real CLI entrypoint parity for canonical and legacy defaults;
- Python-library and MCP facade parity;
- canonical 0/1/2 and legacy 3/4/75 exit behavior;
- pause/resume persistence, reason handling, and mixed-version reads;
- local, GitHub, Jenkins, GitLab, bare, full-depth, and shallow-history contracts;
- successful, contended, and rejected tickets-branch pushes in real temporary git repositories;
- strict workflow failure and best-effort legacy caller controls;
- documentation/help/schema/release-note stale-vocabulary sweeps;
- ADR uniqueness and index coverage;
- repository lint, typecheck, full tests, module-size, packaging, and workflow gates.

The former broken user-guide `--dry-run` example has regression coverage. The CLI whitelist is gone. Current workflows and documentation use canonical bridge vocabulary while compatibility tests keep older environments working.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] The canonical CLI exposes setup, check-access, fsck, status, preview, sync, pause, and resume under `rebar bridge`.
- [x] Argument-less legacy `reconcile` remains dry-run.
- [x] Argument-less canonical `bridge sync` remains live.
- [x] Legacy `bridge-status` remains usable.
- [x] Canonical exit codes are 0, 1, and 2.
- [x] Historical 3, 4, and 75 translations remain available through legacy adapters.
- [x] The Python library exposes the bridge surface.
- [x] The CLI exposes the bridge surface.
- [x] The MCP server exposes the bridge surface.
- [x] brew installation executes the packaged bridge implementation.
- [x] pip installation executes the packaged bridge implementation.
- [x] MCP-server installation executes the packaged bridge implementation.
- [x] Pause state is durable and mixed-version safe.
- [x] Core operations have no required `gh` dependency.
- [x] Local, GitHub, Jenkins, GitLab, and bare environments use the same runner-neutral core.
- [x] Python core owns tickets-branch CAS delivery.
- [x] No workflow-local CAS retry loop remains.
- [x] ADR 0092 has a unique convention-compliant number.
- [x] ADR 0092 is indexed in `docs/adr/README.md`.
- [x] All 20 descendants are closed.
- [x] Every merged code change passed both Gerrit review gates before submission.

## Rollback and residual gaps

The migration is additive and has no persisted-schema backfill. Rollback must restore a workflow delivery implementation before reverting its Python strict adapter, and retained legacy adapters provide the operational fallback. Persistent pause readers accept old and new records, so downgrade remains safe.

Residual-gap sweep: no interface, install path, provider environment, legacy vocabulary, held-out test tier, escalation compromise, or deferred blocking review finding remains undispositioned. Shell snippets remain only where provider configuration requires them and are validated test artifacts; application behavior remains Python-owned.
